text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Swedish state risks losing hundreds of millions of crowns in unpaid value added tax from the early 1990s property crash. The Supreme Court is to decide whether the state can continue to pursue the unpaid taxes.

- Another letter threatening violence if Stockholm wins the 2004 Olympics bid has been sent, again believed to be from the group We Who Built Sweden. This time the letter was sent to an international news agency in London and threatened a massacre of the scale seen at the 1972 Munich Olympics.

- This summer has been one of the warmest this century in Sweden with average temperatures in June, July and August of just under 20 degrees Celsius compared to the average of about 14 degrees and the previous record of about 16 degrees.

- The head of Saab Auto Robert Hendry has written to Prime Minister Goran Persson threatening to break contract with the government if Persson does not take a stand against the Road Authority's decision to only take cars in its fleet with certain petrol consumption. The limits effectively rule all Saab and most Volvo models out of the fleet which both companies say is a negative step for Sweden's car industry.

- A row has erupted between Sweden's car makers and the government over what level of petrol consumption is environmentally acceptable for cars. The Industry Minister has indicated that the Road Authority has gone too far in putting a top limit of 8.6 litres of petrol per 100 kilometres.
- The fall on Stockholm's sharemarket on Monday in the wake of New York's tumble was shortlived, ending less than one percent lower.

- Construction group NCC swung back to profit in the first half of 1997, offsetting a continuing weak building market in Sweden by selling NK Cityfastigheter and Strabruken. The sale of 68 percent of shares in NK Cityfastigheter gave NCC a profit of 160 million crowns. NCC posted a profit of 82 million crowns for the six months against a loss of 82 million last year.

- Forestry company SCA is expanding into Austria, acquiring a 48 percent stake in Welpa company, situated in Margarethen close to Vienna, with an option to acquire a majority share at a later stage. The price was not disclosed.

- Ericsson's smallest cellular phone, the 788 model, has had more technical problems than other company products, according to a survey of eight stores by the newspaper. However Ericsson product manager in Sweden, Per Korner, denies the 788 is a lemon.

- The cost of construction company NCC merging with Siab will be over 450 million crowns which will be absorbed into NCC's balance sheet this financial year. NCC estimated the benefits of the merger to amount to about 400 million crowns a year. The costs and benefits of the deal were higher than previously announced. NCC posted a pre-tax profit of 82 million crowns for the first six months of 1997 but said the Swedish construction market remained weak.

- Netcom made a bigger loss than expected in the first half of 1997, posting a loss of 75 million crowns pretax. But the company's mobile phone operator Comviq continues to increase its number of subscribers.
